raw_doc:
The mode in which the input after the command is read, given the version the command is read
in, or `none` if the command cannot stand in a file, as a declaration of an unsupported version
cannot.

A version declaration is a `set-info` of `:smt-lib-version`; it is read in the version in force
like any other `set-info`, and the input after its `)` is read in the version it declares. `exit`
stops the reading. Every other command, `reset` among them, leaves the mode as it is.

Reading M1: a version declaration changes the mode after its `)`; the value of a declaration is
the number of a supported version. Reading M2: `exit` ends the reading; the input after it is
not read. Reading M3: `reset` does not return to the version the file started in.

Whether the command is a version declaration that names no supported version: a `set-info` of
`:smt-lib-version` whose value is not the number of a supported version, a decimal of no
supported version, a symbol, a list, or no value at all. No script has such a command
(`Tree.Command.modeAfter` gives `none` for it); a parser rejects it after its `)`.

Reading M1: the value of a declaration is the number of a supported version.

`File.From version offset input commands`: with the initial version `version` and the starting
offset `offset`, the input is read as the commands.

Each command is the whitespace and comments before it and its tokens, read in the version in
force. After each command, the rest is read in the version that the command leaves in force;
after `exit`, the rest is not read. A file that is not ended by `exit` ends with whitespace and
comments.

Standard: 2.7 §3.11 Scripts: a script is a sequence of commands. Readings M1, M2 and M3, as
`Tree.Command.modeAfter`.

Property: two s-expressions valid in the same version and written with the same tokens are the
same s-expression.

So in each version, a sequence of tokens is an s-expression in at most one way
(`Syntax.IsSExpr`). If it did not hold, one s-expression would stand for two different trees,
and a parser could not tell which one to hand over.
property: two s-expressions valid in the same version and written with the same tokens are the same s-expression.

raw_doc:
Property: two attributes valid in the same version and written with the same tokens are the
same attribute.

So in each version, a sequence of tokens is an attribute in at most one way
(`Syntax.IsAttribute`). If it did not hold, one attribute would stand for two different trees,
and a parser could not tell which one to hand over.
property: two attributes valid in the same version and written with the same tokens are the same attribute.

raw_doc:
Property: two sorts valid in the same version and written with the same tokens are the same
sort.

So in each version, a sequence of tokens is a sort in at most one way (`Syntax.IsSort`). If it did
not hold, one sort would stand for two different trees, and a parser could not tell which one to
hand over.
property: two sorts valid in the same version and written with the same tokens are the same sort.

raw_doc:
Property: two terms valid in the same version and written with the same tokens are the same
term.

So in each version, a sequence of tokens is a term in at most one way (`Syntax.IsTerm`). If it
did not hold, one term would stand for two different trees, and a parser could not tell which
one to hand over.
property: two terms valid in the same version and written with the same tokens are the same term.

raw_doc:
Property: two commands valid in the same version and written with the same tokens are the same
command.

So in each version, a sequence of tokens is a command in at most one way (`Syntax.IsCommand`).
The version matters: `(check-sat-assuming (p))` is written the same as a command with a
list of terms, valid in 2.7, and as one with a list of propositional literals, valid in 2.6, and
only one of them is valid in each version.
property: two commands valid in the same version and written with the same tokens are the same command.

raw_doc:
Property: every file has at most one reading.

This does not follow from `CommandsOneToOne` alone: a file can change the version in which the
rest of it is read, so it also rests on each command determining the version that the rest is
read in.
property: every file has at most one reading.

raw_doc:
Property: a lexer fed the characters of a command, up to its `)`, has handed over all its
tokens and holds nothing back.

So reading can stop at the end of a command and start again, possibly in the version the command
switches to, without a token of the command waiting for what follows it. A command ends with its
`)`, which needs no delimiter.
property: a lexer fed the characters of a command, up to its `)`, has handed over all its tokens and holds nothing back.

raw_doc:
`Script version commands`: with the initial version `version`, the commands make a script: each is
valid in the version in force where it starts, and only the last one may stop the reading.

The commands of a file make a script (`File`); a script is what a parser of tokens is given.

raw_doc:
What a lexical token stands for, and for a symbol whether it was quoted.

Standard: 2.7 §3.1 Symbols, as `SyntaxToken`.

Property: the token is a parenthesis, or the character after it is in the input.

A token other than a parenthesis needs a delimiter after it (`Tokenization.Delimited`, Reading
L1), so a lexer can tell that the token ends where it does only once it has read the character
after it. A parenthesis needs no delimiter.
property: the token is a parenthesis, or the character after it is in the input.

raw_doc:
Property: `start` is the longest start of `input` that is viable.

Up to the end of `start`, characters may still follow that make a valid input; past it, none
can. While the input is `Viable`, `start` is all of it; once it is not, `start` ends where it
stopped being viable. Of `(a #q`, it is `(a #`: `#x1` could follow, but nothing can follow
`(a #q`. A lexer fed in slices has read such a start of the input.
property: `start` is the longest start of `input` that is viable.

raw_doc:
Property: no characters that follow the input can change the tokens, and the character after
each of them but a parenthesis is in the input.

These are tokens that a lexer fed the input in slices may hand over: they are `Determined`,
and their delimiter has been read (`DelimiterSeen`). After `(x |abc|`, `(` and `x` are ready,
but `|abc|` is not: it is determined, but the character after it has not been read.
property: no characters that follow the input can change the tokens, and the character after each of them but a parenthesis is in the input.

raw_doc:
Property: the tokens are ready to be handed over, and no longer list of tokens is ready.

These are all the tokens that a lexer fed the input in slices may hand over, so a lexer that
hands them over holds nothing back. On an input that is not `Viable`, every list is
determined, so no list is maximal.
property: the tokens are ready to be handed over, and no longer list of tokens is ready.

raw_doc:
Property: the input has ended, and it has a tokenisation.

The lexer has then read the input to its end without failing, and the end of the input
delimits the last token, so every token of the tokenisation is ready. An input that has ended
without a tokenisation of its own is not complete, even when it is `Viable`: on `(a "ab`, the
end of the input does not complete the string literal.
property: the input has ended, and it has a tokenisation.

raw_doc:
Property: a lexer has failed exactly when the input can no longer be valid.

The lexer is fed the slices, and then the end of the input if the input has ended.

Before the end, characters may still follow: while the input is `Viable`, they may make a valid
input of it, so the lexer must not fail; once it is not, none can, so the lexer must have
failed. After the end, nothing can follow, so the lexer must have failed exactly when the input
has no tokenisation. `"ab` is viable, so a lexer fails on it only at the end.

Reading L8: the input need not be a `SourceFile`.
property: a lexer has failed exactly when the input can no longer be valid.

raw_doc:
Property: the input has a tokenisation, and a lexer has handed over its tokens followed by the
end-of-file token.

The lexer is fed the slices and then the end of the input. This is what the lexer must have
handed over when the input is `Complete`: the end of the input delimits the last token, so every
token is ready.

Reading L8: the input need not be a `SourceFile`.
property: the input has a tokenisation, and a lexer has handed over its tokens followed by the end-of-file token.

raw_doc:
Property: a lexer has handed over the maximal list of ready tokens on the longest viable start
of the input, and nothing else.

The lexer is fed the slices, and then the end of the input if the input has ended. This is what
the lexer must have handed over when the input is not `Complete`. `start` is that longest
viable start (`LongestViableStart`), all of the input while it is viable. So the lexer holds no
token back, hands none over before it is ready, and hands none over from where the input
stopped being viable on.

The end of an input that is not complete releases no token: on `(a "ab`, the lexer has handed
over `(` and `a`, at the end as before it. Nor does the end of the input delimit a token after
the input stopped being viable: on `(a bc"`, the lexer has handed over `(` and `a`, and not
`bc`, since it read `"` after `bc` and not the end.

Reading L8: the input need not be a `SourceFile`.
property: a lexer has handed over the maximal list of ready tokens on the longest viable start of the input, and nothing else.

raw_doc:
Property: a lexer has handed over the tokens that are ready, and nothing else.

The lexer is fed the slices, and then the end of the input if the input has ended. The property
is `HandsOverAll` if the input is `Complete`, and `HandsOverMaximal` if it is not.
property: a lexer has handed over the tokens that are ready, and nothing else.

raw_doc:
Property: a lexer is correct on every version and every input, ended or not.

It is `FailsCorrectly` and `HandsOverCorrectly`.
property: a lexer is correct on every version and every input, ended or not.

raw_doc:
Property: `later` has handed over what `before` had, and possibly more, and has failed if
`before` had.
property: `later` has handed over what `before` had, and possibly more, and has failed if `before` had.

raw_doc:
Property: what a lexer has done extends as it is fed more slices, and as it is fed the end of
the input.

What a lexer hands over is never taken back, so a later command cannot change what a consumer
has done with the tokens of an earlier one. The end of the input only releases what waited for it.
property: what a lexer has done extends as it is fed more slices, and as it is fed the end of the input.

raw_doc:
Property: a lexer has handed over `handed` without failing exactly when `handed` is the tokens
of the tokenisation of the input followed by the end-of-file token. The lexer is fed the slices
and then the end of the input.

So it fails exactly when the input has no tokenisation. This is what the standard asks of a
whole input.

Reading L8: the input need not be a `SourceFile`.
property: a lexer has handed over `handed` without failing exactly when `handed` is the tokens of the tokenisation of the input followed by the end-of-file token. The lexer is fed the slices and then the end of the input.

raw_doc:
Property: characters whose tokenisation ends with a `)` at their end are handed over whole, and
the characters followed by more are tokenised as the two parts read on their own.

This is a property of the formalism alone. A command ends with a `)`, which needs no
delimiter, so its end is a point where reading can stop and start again, possibly in another
version: a lexer fed the command holds nothing of it back, and the input after it is tokenised
as an input of its own, its tokens moved by the length of what came before.
property: characters whose tokenisation ends with a `)` at their end are handed over whole, and the characters followed by more are tokenised as the two parts read on their own.

raw_doc:
Property: the consumer does not continue on the end-of-file token.

Every consumer breaks at the end of the input at the latest, with a result, or fails. It is an
obligation on the consumer: a lexer handed a consumer that continues there owes nothing.
property: the consumer does not continue on the end-of-file token.

raw_doc:
Property: the end of the input resets the version and the discarding.

This is the session of a lexer created with the version `start` that reaches the outcome with
the tokens taken. If the outcome finishes the input, the version is reset to `start` and the
lexer no longer discards; otherwise the version and the discarding are as given.
property: the end of the input resets the version and the discarding.

raw_doc:
Property: the input after a version switch is read on its own, in the new version.

This is what a lexer hands over to the collector from the offset of the input on, in the
version: what `feed` does with the input from the offset on, read on its own and located in the
whole input. `ReadsOnItsOwn` and `ComposesAtClose` say that reading on its own loses nothing
where the switch is at a `)`.
property: the input after a version switch is read on its own, in the new version.

raw_doc:
Property: a lexer hands a concrete consumer the layout from the offset of the input on, up to the
first character that starts no layout. Each piece is an entry of its own, handed over once it is
complete.

A piece is a run of white space characters, complete once a character after it is not
one, or a comment with its line-breaking character, complete once that character is read;
either is complete once the input has ended. The content of a run is its characters, that of a
comment its characters after the `;`, with the line-breaking character. Between two tokens, the
pieces reach from the one to the other.
property: a lexer hands a concrete consumer the layout from the offset of the input on, up to the first character that starts no layout. Each piece is an entry of its own, handed over once it is complete.

raw_doc:
Property: from the offset of the input on, a lexer hands a consumer the tokens, and a concrete
consumer also the layout before the first token and after each token.

The tokens it hands over from there, and whether it fails after them, are given.
property: from the offset of the input on, a lexer hands a consumer the tokens, and a concrete consumer also the layout before the first token and after each token.

raw_doc:
Property: the entries ready from the offset of the input on, and whether the lexer fails after
them, are those of the input from there, read on its own in the version (`segment`).
property: the entries ready from the offset of the input on, and whether the lexer fails after them, are those of the input from there, read on its own in the version (`segment`).

raw_doc:
Property: after an entry, the lexer goes on with the entries ready after it in the version in
force after it.

The entries ready after an entry that ends at the offset, and whether the lexer fails after them:
those ready after it as before, given as `rest` and `failed`, unless the consumer switched the
version at the entry, in which case the input after the entry is read on its own in the new
version. A switch is allowed after any entry.
property: after an entry, the lexer goes on with the entries ready after it in the version in force after it.

raw_doc:
Property: where a lexer stands after the consumer broke with the result at an entry that ends at
`location`, given the entries ready after it and whether the lexer fails after them.

The first entry handed over after the break is `UnexpectedTrailingToken`, at its start. If that
entry is the end-of-file token, the input has ended and the result is returned instead. If no
entry follows, the lexer fails if it fails after the entries, with a lexical error, and otherwise
holds the result.
property: where a lexer stands after the consumer broke with the result at an entry that ends at `location`, given the entries ready after it and whether the lexer fails after them.
`Runs feed consumer start input ended version ready failed taken session`: from a point of its run, a lexer ends in `session`. At that point:

raw_doc:
Property: a lexer does with a consumer that breaks at the end of the input what `Runs` states.

`Runs` starts from the start of the input with nothing taken, and is relative to what the lexer
hands over to the collector. The lexer is fed the slices, and then the end of the input if the
input has ended.
property: a lexer does with a consumer that breaks at the end of the input what `Runs` states.

raw_doc:
Property: after an input on which the lexer finished, the lexer does on what it is fed next
what a new lexer created with the same version does.

So the end of the input resets everything: the version, the discarding, the held result, the
partial token, and the locations, which start again at zero.
property: after an input on which the lexer finished, the lexer does on what it is fed next what a new lexer created with the same version does.

raw_doc:
Property: a lexer is correct with every consumer on every version and every input, ended or not:
it is `Correct` with the collector, handles every consumer that breaks at the end of the input,
and is reset by the end of the input.
property: a lexer is correct with every consumer on every version and every input, ended or not: it is `Correct` with the collector, handles every consumer that breaks at the end of the input, and is reset by the end of the input.

raw_doc:
Property: a lexer that recovers from errors drops the held result on any error after the break,
and then returns no result at the end of the input.

A value is confirmed only at the end of the input, so an error after it, `UnexpectedTrailingToken`
among them, leaves nothing to confirm.
property: a lexer that recovers from errors drops the held result on any error after the break, and then returns no result at the end of the input.

raw_doc:
Property: every input has at most one tokenisation.

This is a property of the formalism alone. `BSmtLibSpec.Facts.Lexicon` proves it as
`Lexicon.unique`. If it did not hold, the formalism would let one input stand for two
different sequences of tokens, and no lexer could hand over the right one.
property: every input has at most one tokenisation.

raw_doc:
Property: some input that starts with the given characters has a tokenisation.

A lexer fed an input in slices does not know the characters that follow. It can report an
error only once the characters fed are not viable: until then, the characters still to come may
yet make them the start of a valid input.
property: some input that starts with the given characters has a tokenisation.

raw_doc:
Property: all tokenisations of inputs that start with the given characters start with the
given tokens.

No characters that follow can change these tokens, so a lexer fed an input in slices can hand
them over without waiting for the rest of the input. The empty list always qualifies, and if
the given characters are not `Viable`, every list does.
property: all tokenisations of inputs that start with the given characters start with the given tokens.

raw_doc:
Property: characters read from any offset, in any version, are tokenised as they are on their
own, their tokens moved to that offset.

This is a property of the formalism alone. Where reading stops and starts again, possibly
in another version, the characters after the stop are read as an input of their own; without
this property, where they stand in the whole input could change their tokens.
property: characters read from any offset, in any version, are tokenised as they are on their own, their tokens moved to that offset.

raw_doc:
The delimitation rule: a token other than a parenthesis is followed by the end of the
input, a white space character, a parenthesis or the `;` that starts a comment. The standard
does not state how adjacent tokens are separated; this is the strict reading, under which
`1.5` is one decimal rather than `1` followed by `.5`, and `"a"b` is not an input.

Reading L1: a token other than a parenthesis is followed by a delimiter.

`Tokenization.From version offset input tokens`: with the starting offset `offset`, the tokens
are a tokenisation of the input.

Standard: 2.7 §3.1: the only lexical function of whitespace is to break the source text into
tokens. Readings L1 and L2.

`Tokenization version input tokens`: the tokens are a tokenisation of the input.

raw_doc:
⟨white_space_char⟩: 9 (tab), 10 (line feed), 13 (carriage return) or 32 (space).

Standard: 2.7 §3.1 White Space Characters; App. B ⟨white_space_char⟩.

⟨printable_char⟩: a character from 32 to 126, or from 128 on.

Standard: 2.7 §3.1 Printable Characters; App. B ⟨printable_char⟩.

Reading L8: In 2.0, the characters from 128 on are excluded by `SourceFile`, not here.

⟨digit⟩: a character from 48 to 57 (`0` to `9`).

Standard: 2.7 §3.1 Digits; App. B ⟨digit⟩.

⟨letter⟩: a character from 65 to 90 (`A` to `Z`) or from 97 to 122 (`a` to `z`).

Standard: 2.7 §3.1 Letters; App. B ⟨letter⟩.

Reading L3: 2.5 App. B writes ⟨letter⟩ as `A | ··· | A | a | ··· | z`; this
follows §3.1, which gives 65 to 90.

A line-breaking character: 10 or 13.

Standard: 2.7 §3.1 Comments: the line-breaking characters 10 and 13.

A comment: a sequence that begins with `;` and ends with the first subsequent
line-breaking character.

Standard: 2.7 §3.1 Comments.

A comment that runs to the end of the input. The line-breaking character terminates a
comment; a comment need not be terminated to be one.

Reading L2: a comment may run to the end of the input.

Whitespace: comments and white space characters, outside string literals and symbols.

Standard: 2.7 §3.1: both comments and consecutive white space characters are whitespace.
original_extractor_standard: 2.7 §3.1: both comments and consecutive white space characters are whitespace.

Whitespace at the end of the input, which may end with a comment that runs to the end.

Reading L2: whitespace at the end of the input may end with a comment that runs to the end.

⟨numeral⟩: the digit `0`, or a non-empty sequence of digits not starting with `0`.

Standard: 2.7 §3.1 Numerals; App. B ⟨numeral⟩.

⟨decimal⟩: ⟨numeral⟩`.``0`*⟨numeral⟩.

Standard: 2.7 §3.1 Decimals; App. B ⟨decimal⟩.

⟨hexadecimal⟩: `#x` followed by a non-empty sequence of digits and of letters from `A` to
`F`, capitalised or not.

Standard: 2.7 §3.1 Hexadecimals; App. B ⟨hexadecimal⟩.

⟨binary⟩: `#b` followed by a non-empty sequence of the characters `0` and `1`.

Standard: 2.7 §3.1 Binaries; App. B ⟨binary⟩.

⟨string⟩ from 2.5 on: a sequence of printable and white space characters delimited by `"`.
A `"` within it occurs only duplicated, as `""`.

Standard: 2.5, 2.6 and 2.7 §3.1 String literals; App. B ⟨string⟩.

What the inside of a string literal from 2.5 on stands for: each `""` stands for `"`.

Standard: 2.5, 2.6 and 2.7 §3.1 String literals.

⟨string⟩ in 2.0: a sequence of printable characters delimited by `"`, possibly containing
the escape sequences `\"` and `\\`; a backslash before any other character is just a
backslash, and the character after it is taken with it. In 2.0, the printable characters
include tab and the line-breaking characters: its rules for quoted symbols say so once and

The regular expression for a token category.

Standard: 2.7 §3.1, as `Category`.

A token of an input.

Standard: 2.7 §3.1 lexical tokens.

Formalism: we record the token using its category, offset, and text (not its content).
formalism: we record the token using its category, offset, and text (not its content).

raw_doc:
The token content.

The content is what the token stands for: a string literal without the enclosing
quotes and escapes, the name of a quoted symbol without its bars, a keyword
without its colon, the digits of a hexadecimal or binary without `#x` or `#b`,
and otherwise the characters of the token.

stand for.

raw_doc:
Property: the traversal of a script takes exactly what a parser receives for it, each item
arriving and then processed, in order.

So the traversal places its calls among the very tokens the grammar writes the script as, and
nothing in the traversal repeats the grammar without the grammar checking it.
property: the traversal of a script takes exactly what a parser receives for it, each item arriving and then processed, in order.

raw_doc:
Property: two scripts with the same initial version whose traversals make the same calls are the
same script.

So the calls lose nothing: a handler is told every construct of the script, in a form from which
the script can be rebuilt. Only the whitespace between the tokens is not told.
property: two scripts with the same initial version whose traversals make the same calls are the same script.

raw_doc:
Property: what the traversal of a script has done before an item arrives, and before it is
processed, depends only on the items before it.

So what a parser has done is well defined where its input stops: when its producer has no
further token, it is what the traversal of any script that continues the input does before the
next item arrives; when it rejects an item, what that traversal does before the item is
processed. Without this, a parser could not know which calls to make before the tokens that
decide them, and would have to guess.
property: what the traversal of a script has done before an item arrives, and before it is processed, depends only on the items before it.

raw_doc:
`Takes version commands items ending`: with the initial version `version`, a parser takes the
items for the commands, and then ends as `ending` says. There are two cases:

- the commands are a script, the items are what a parser receives for it (`received`), and the
  parser finishes;
- the commands are valid up to a version declaration that names no supported version, which ends
  them; the items are their tokens up to that declaration's `)`, and the parser fails there with
  `unsupportedVersion`.

Standard: 2.7 §3.11 Scripts. Readings M1, M2 and M3, as `Tree.Command.modeAfter`.
original_extractor_standard: 2.7 §3.11 Scripts. Readings M1, M2 and M3, as `Tree.Command.modeAfter`.

raw_doc:
The version in force at the item at position `count` (from zero) of what a parser takes for the
commands, with the initial version: the version a declaration declares holds from the item after
its `)` on.

Reading M1: a version declaration changes the mode after its `)`.

Property: a parser takes what a parser takes for a script, or for commands that a declaration of
a version that is not supported ends, as the traversal does.

Given items that stand for what it takes, the parser has made, on any start of them, the
traversal's events before the next item arrives. When it has been given all of them, it ends as
`Takes` says; otherwise it waits for the next item.

So a parser rejects no item that some script continues with, and it rejects a declaration of a
version that is not supported after its `)`, as it rejects a version that its policy does not
allow.
property: a parser takes what a parser takes for a script, or for commands that a declaration of a version that is not supported ends, as the traversal does.

raw_doc:
Property: a parser rejects the first item that no script continues with.

Let the items before position `count` stand for the start of what a parser takes for a script,
or for commands that a declaration of a version that is not supported ends, and let the item at
`count` be one that no script continues with. Then the parser takes the items up to that one and
rejects it. Before processing it, the parser has made the traversal's events before the item's
processing, where a `)` gets none of the calls due at its arrival (`eventsBeforeProcessingOf`).
Processing the item makes no call, so it is the last event of the run.

A lexer hands over a reserved word only if the version in force reserves it, and a parser
relies on that; so the rejected item is taken to be one that a lexer can hand over in the version
in force. The items before it are such items too, as they stand for items of a valid script.

After `exit`, a parser asks its producer to discard the rest of the input, and relies on that
too: a producer that honours the request hands over nothing after it but the end of the input. So
where the traversal has asked for the discarding before the rejected item, that item is taken to
be the end of the input.
property: a parser rejects the first item that no script continues with.

raw_doc:
The item is one that a lexer can hand over in the version, as far as a parser can tell: a
reserved word is one that the version reserves.

Standard: 2.7 §3.1 Reserved words; ⟨reserved⟩ of each version.

Property: a reader reads a file to its end: it tells the handler the calls for the file's
commands, and finishes.

The reader is fed the file in any slices, and then the end of the input.
property: a reader reads a file to its end: it tells the handler the calls for the file's commands, and finishes.

raw_doc:
Property: a reader finishes only if its input is a file.

The reader is fed the input in any slices, and then the end of the input.
property: a reader finishes only if its input is a file.

raw_doc:
Property: the calls for the commands of a file determine the file's initial version and its
commands.

So the handler is told the whole file but for three things that no call carries: the whitespace
and the comments; everything after `exit`, which is not read, and which a caller takes from the
input where the lexer began to discard; and, in 2.0, how a string literal is spelled, since two
spellings can stand for the same characters (`"\a"` and `"\\a"`). `BSmtLibSpec.Facts.Reader`
proves it.
property: the calls for the commands of a file determine the file's initial version and its commands.

raw_doc:
Property: on every input, ended or not, a reader does what a correct lexer does with a correct
parser as its consumer.

The lexer is correct with every consumer (`Lexer.CorrectWithConsumers`). The parser follows the
traversal and rejects the first item that no script continues with (`FollowsTheTraversal`,
`RejectsFirstUnviable`); it takes each token that a lexer can hand over in some version for what
the token stands for. The handler is told the parser's calls on the tokens the lexer handed
over, and the reader finishes when the lexer does. Until the lexer hands over the first token,
the handler is told nothing, not even the version.
property: on every input, ended or not, a reader does what a correct lexer does with a correct parser as its consumer.
